opus-5.5.text:
That's a comparison I get asked about quite a lot, and honestly I think about it myself, because Cursor's growth has been incredible. It's inspiring to watch.

But I try to be careful not to draw the wrong lessons from it. Cursor sits on top of a market that's enormous and already very mature. There are tens of millions of software developers, they already spend all day inside an editor, and they already understand the value of a tool that makes them faster. So when a much better coding experience shows up, adoption can be explosive. The workflow is there, the budget is there, and the habit is there.

3D is a different story. The number of people who are professional 3D artists is much smaller. And the people who *want* 3D content, like indie game developers, people doing 3D printing, educators, e-commerce, XR creators, a lot of them have never been able to make it themselves, because traditional 3D tools are really hard. Learning Blender or Maya well takes years. So for Meshy, a big part of the job isn't just making existing professionals faster. It's expanding who gets to be a 3D creator at all. That's more like creating a market than capturing one, and creating a market usually takes more patience.

There's also a technical difference. Code is text, and large language models got really good at text first. 3D is much harder. You care about geometry, topology, UVs, textures, rigging, whether the model actually works in a game engine or prints cleanly. The quality bar for "production-ready" is high, and we're still pushing that frontier every month. In a sense, 3D generation today is a bit like where code generation was a couple of years earlier. The curve is steep, but we're earlier on it.

So how do I see our position? I don't think we need to be Cursor. I think we need to be the best at what we do, which is turning ideas into usable 3D assets as easily as possible, and to keep compounding. We focus a lot on really listening to users, shipping fast, and making the output actually usable in real pipelines, not just pretty in a demo.

And I'm quite optimistic, because I believe 3D content demand is going to grow enormously: games, simulation, robotics, spatial computing, AR and VR. When that wave comes, the bottleneck is going to be content creation. If we've built the best tool and the strongest community by then, I think the growth will come. Maybe not with the exact same shape as Cursor's, but in a way that fits our market.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Cursor’s mature market with Meshy’s earlier market, but does not say Cursor’s growth came from a lucky market choice or that sustaining success requires execution ability.

r002.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s current focus on usable 3D assets, user feedback, fast shipping, and real pipelines, then presents its tool and community as a foundation for growth when future 3D demand expands.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a comparison I get asked about a lot, and honestly I think it's flattering but also a little misleading. Cursor is riding one of the biggest tailwinds in the history of software: every developer in the world already writes code every day, the output is text, the feedback loop is instant, and the models got good at it extremely fast. So when the product clicked, adoption was almost frictionless. You don't have to convince anyone that they need code.

Meshy is in a different situation. 3D is a much smaller professional market today, the workflows are heavier, and "good enough" is harder to define. A game studio cares about topology, UVs, poly counts, how an asset rigs and animates, whether it fits an art direction. A model that produces something that looks nice in a turntable video is not the same thing as a model that produces something you can ship. So our growth curve is going to look different, and I think it should. We spent a lot of time on the unglamorous parts: mesh quality, texturing, retopology, making the output actually usable in Unity, Unreal, Blender.

Where I think the comparison is useful is in the shape of the opportunity, not the speed. Cursor showed that if you make creation ten times cheaper, the market doesn't stay the same size, it expands. We're already seeing that. A lot of our users aren't traditional 3D artists. They're indie developers, designers, people doing 3D printing, educators, folks who never would have opened Maya. If 3D content becomes as easy to make as an image, the number of people making it goes up by orders of magnitude, and then 3D stops being a niche.

So I'm not trying to be Cursor for 3D in terms of velocity. I'm trying to be the company that's still standing and still the quality leader when that expansion actually happens. I'd rather grow with the market than sprint ahead of it with a product that professionals don't trust yet. Patience is a competitive advantage here, because the hard technical problems are the moat.

r001.rationale: The response attributes Cursor’s growth to favorable market conditions and a frictionless product, but does not argue that sustaining success will eventually require execution ability.

r002.rationale: It describes Meshy’s work on usable, professional-quality 3D tools as a foundation for pursuing the future expansion of the 3D market.

astra-6.text:
I think Cursor is a useful comparison, but coding and 3D creation are very different markets. Developers already spend much of their day writing code, so a tool that makes that workflow faster has a very direct path to adoption. With Meshy, we need to make 3D creation easier while also helping people understand what they can do with it.

So I wouldn’t judge our position just by whether we grow at the same speed as Cursor. The question is whether we’re making something that people can actually use in their work. There’s value in helping existing 3D artists, but there’s also an opportunity to let people create things they couldn’t create before. That’s what I’d focus on.

r001.rationale: The response says Cursor and Meshy operate in different markets and that Meshy should be judged by usefulness. It does not discuss luck in Cursor’s market choice or the need for execution to sustain success.

r002.rationale: The response mentions value for existing 3D artists and an opportunity to enable new creators, but does not present Meshy’s existing business foundation as a position from which to pursue those opportunities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Cursor is a really interesting reference point, but the markets are different. Developers already spend a lot of time writing code, so if you make that workflow better, there’s a very clear reason to use the product every day.

For Meshy, the question is how we make creating 3D content that useful and accessible. We need to help people who already work in 3D, but there’s also an opportunity to bring in people who have ideas and haven’t had the skills to build them.

So I wouldn’t assume we’ll follow the same growth curve. What excites me is the possibility of expanding who can create in 3D. But that depends on making the output useful enough that people keep coming back.

r001.rationale: The response compares the markets and says Meshy may not follow Cursor’s growth curve, but it does not discuss luck in Cursor’s market choice or the need for execution to sustain success.

r002.rationale: It mentions serving people who already work in 3D and expanding access to new creators, but does not present Meshy’s existing business foundation as a base for pursuing future opportunities.
